episodes.title: Meet Sena and Daniel: What AI Can't Do for You
Reading Emotions on a Video Call

brief_data.summary: On a voice-only call at ten in the morning in Tokyo, Wendell is angry that Mark still wants a rough cut of region three "next Friday" after he said three weeks three times, and Sena's first instinct, "I'm sure Mark didn't mean it like that," makes it worse until she says back what she heard in his words. Daniel shares Seehausen and colleagues' small Berlin study, where paraphrasing during a real conflict left people feeling less negative and speaking more quietly, and Weger and colleagues' study of 115 students, where active listening made people feel more understood than advice or simple acknowledgments. He tells the story of Bram, who told him "You're answering a question I didn't ask," and they compare Japanese aizuchi and "maa maa" with the American "What I'm hearing is..." Today's challenge: when someone sounds upset today, say back what you heard in one sentence, in their words, before you reassure or advise.
brief_data.hook:
A coworker calls you, angry: "I said three weeks. Three times. Nobody asks what it takes." You say "I'm sure he didn't mean it," and it gets worse.
Learn the one sentence to say first when someone is upset: their words, said back, before any advice or reassurance.

brief_data.summary: On Monday morning in Tokyo, Sena opens the data-check log to get one detail right: Kenta quietly re-ran the region check on every number in her slides at 7:12 a.m. before Thursday's presentation, and all she wrote back was one word, "Thanks!" Daniel shares Kumar and Epley's finding that people who express gratitude underestimate how happy and how surprised by the details the recipient will feel, and Algoe, Kurtz and Hilaire's study where "you" sentences about the helper mattered more than "it helped me." He tells the story of the eight identical thank-you cards he once wrote, and they compare Japan's "sumimasen" and "otsukaresama" with America's quick "Thanks!! You rock!" Today's challenge: send one specific thank-you message today.
brief_data.hook:
A coworker quietly double-checked your numbers before a big presentation, and all you wrote back was one word: "Thanks!" Sound familiar?
Learn a three-part thank-you (what they did, the impact, what it showed you) that people actually remember.
brief_data.thumb_sub: Say What They Did, Make It Specific

brief_data.summary: On Tuesday morning on a bench by the moat in Tokyo, Sena counts the stress signals in her notebook margins: thirty-four notes in two weeks, twenty-two about speaking English, zero about the numbers, and six workdays with no note at all, two days after telling her mother these were the hardest two weeks of her life. In the Season Two finale, Daniel shares Kahneman and colleagues' Day Reconstruction Method study, where 909 employed women rebuilt one workday scene by scene, and Diener, Lucas and Scollon's review showing that happiness set points aren't neutral, differ between people, and can change. He tells the story of the terrible March when he almost quit managing, and they compare Japan's "daijoubu" with America's "Great!" Today's challenge: write one word a day for a week and look back.
brief_data.hook:
You're sure the last two weeks were the worst of your life. But can you remember the quiet days?
Learn how one word a day shows your real emotional baseline: your usual weather, not your worst storm.
brief_data.thumb_sub: One Word a Day, Find Your Usual Weather
thumb_notes: Usual weather, not the worst storm
